### 2.1 Remote Labor Index (remote-labor-index)

`data/benchmarks/society-econ-law/remote-labor-index.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-08 · last verified 2026-11-08

*Agents attempt 240 real paid freelance projects; human evaluators judge whether a client would accept the work.*

A benchmark from the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI built from 240 end-to-end remote freelance projects, mostly sourced through Upwork from 358 freelancers who sold their past work samples, plus 33 permissioned examples of digital work found online. Each project is a brief, a directory of input files and the professional's own deliverable, with the time and price the professional reported (a mean of 28.9 hours; $143,991 in all). The projects span 23 Upwork categories, among them 3D and CAD, architecture, graphic and product design, video and animation, audio, game development and data visualisation, so deliverables come in dozens of file formats. An agent receives the brief and inputs, with a prompt listing the formats the evaluation platform can render, and works unattended. Trained evaluators compare its deliverable with the human one on a three-point scale, from the standpoint of a reasonable client, and the majority of three verdicts decides. The headline automation rate is the share of projects whose AI deliverable is judged at least as good as the professional's; the paper also fits an Elo rating from pairwise comparisons between agents and reports dollars earned and "autoflation". 230 projects are a private test set, which Scale Labs evaluates and ranks on its leaderboard; 10 projects and the evaluation platform are public. The best agent scored 2.5% at release; the board read here is topped at 21.25%.

#### remote-labor-index · Domain and capabilities

- `domain.primary` = society-econ-law/economically-valuable-work · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: The projects are real paid freelance work, each with the professional's own deliverable and its reported price, and the score is whether human evaluators judge the AI deliverable at least as good as that professional's, which is the leaf's definition (tasks from real paid occupations, scored by expert comparison against human work product). The taxonomy cites this benchmark as the family's example.
  > Automation rate: The percentage of projects for which the AI deliverable is judged by human evaluators to complete the project at least as well as the human deliverable.
- `domain.secondary` = agents-tooluse/long-horizon-autonomy · [S3][remote-labor-index-s3]
  - why: Each project is an extended unattended episode (professionals report a mean of 28.9 hours, and the 2026 setup allows an agent up to 24 hours of wall-clock time per project), carried out by an agent in a CLI or computer-use environment. It is secondary because what is scored is the deliverable's acceptability as commissioned work, not the operation (see domain\_considered\_and\_rejected).
  > Each project gets up to 24 hours of wall-clock time
- `capability` = autonomy · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: The agent works the project through unattended; the base prompt forbids questions, and the brief and inputs are cleaned so that no further information is needed. Projects needing interaction with a client were excluded.
  > Read the brief attached and create only the deliverables described. Do not ask any questions.
- `capability` = context-integration · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: The professional who did the work supplies the brief and the input files (a voiceover to animate, a ring sketch to model, data to visualise), and a deliverable that ignores them fails the brief.
  > This ensures the brief and input files contain sufficient information to complete the project.
- `capability` = generation-fidelity · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: The produced artifact is judged against a target, the brief and the professional's reference deliverable, by human judgement of whether it satisfies the brief as well as the reference does.
  > Evaluators digest the project context (brief, input files, human deliverable) and compare the human and AI deliverables
- `evaluation_method` = human-expert-eval · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: Human evaluators trained on the protocol rate each AI deliverable one by one, and their majority verdicts are the result.
  > We use majority voting across three independent evaluations to determine the final judgment.
- `designed_for_subjects` = agent-scaffold, full-product-pipeline · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: The protocol fixes no environment or agent architecture, and each result belongs to a model inside a chosen scaffold. The paper ran two shipped agents as delivered (ChatGPT agent, Manus) beside models in Scale AI's computer-use scaffold or OpenHands, the leaderboard keeps each agent's best environment, and the 2026 results run each model family in its developer's own coding agent with computer use added.
  > We do not mandate a specific execution environment or agent architecture.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `agents-tooluse/computer-use-gui` · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: The family's near miss, OSWorld 2.0, is economically valuable computer work scored as autonomous operation of an interface. RLI does not score the operation at all. The protocol leaves the environment and agent architecture to the entrant (the paper ran CLI and computer-use scaffolds and integrated products side by side), the evaluators judge the deliverable rather than how it was produced, and the verdict is whether a reasonable client would accept it against a professional's paid work, which is the economic value of the output, the family's own discriminant. The paper sets itself against computer-use evaluations.
  > revealing a stark gap between progress on computer use evaluations and the ability to perform real and economically valuable work
- `domain` not `agents-tooluse/operating-system-tasks` · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: The CLI scaffold (OpenHands) acts through a shell, and agents-tooluse was weighed as primary through its inclusion test (what an autonomous loop achieved, with the grader checking the result it returned). The grader here is not a check of a machine's end state or of a returned result against a goal but a client's acceptance judged against human work product, and the paper grounds the measure in economic transactions; the family is kept as a secondary through long-horizon-autonomy.
  > In contrast to prior benchmarks, RLI measures the automation ability of AI agents on end-to-end projects sourced from real-world work in remote labor markets, thereby grounding the evaluation in actual economic transactions.
- `domain` not `society-econ-law/legal-document` · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: Legal work is not the subject; most legal categories were excluded from collection.
  > Most legal categories were excluded due to PII concerns.
- `capability` not `long-horizon-execution` · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: Professionals take a mean of 28.9 hours per project, but no source shows that an intermediate error leaves full success unattainable; files can be regenerated and revised within the budget, and the 2026 setup adds a critic loop for revision.
  > with a mean of 28.9 hours and median of 11.5 hours
- `capability` not `self-correction` · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: The paper names failure to verify and fix one's own work as a common failure, and the 2026 setup runs a worker-critic loop, but the loop belongs to the scaffold and no score measures revision.
  > many failures stem from AI agents being unable to verify the correctness of their work and fix mistakes
- `evaluation_method` not `human-crowd-eval` · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: The paper describes its evaluators as trained workers and subject experts, and the leaderboard as trained experts; no qualification requirement is stated (see review\_checks).
  > Thus, all evaluations are performed manually by trained workers and subject experts.
- `evaluation_method` not `pairwise-preference-elo` · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: The paper fits a Bradley-Terry rating (called Elo, with the human baseline at 1,000) from pairwise comparisons of agents' deliverables, but the leaderboard and CAIS report only the automation rate, a win or tie against one fixed reference, which the term's exclusion covers.
  > Elo: A score capturing the relative performance of different AI agents.
- `evaluation_method` not `rubric-graded` · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: Per-project rubrics were tried and dropped for a holistic judgement.
  > we found granular per-project rubrics were often insufficient for capturing project completion
- `evaluation_method` not `model-graded-judge` · [S3][remote-labor-index-s3]
  - why: No score comes from a model. The paper judges automated evaluation infeasible, and CAIS's 2026 agentic judge overstated the newest models' automation rates two to three times, so it was not adopted.
  > That makes an automated grader useful for tracking relative progress, but not a substitute for human evaluation of absolute capability.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `model-in-benchmark-harness` · [S4][remote-labor-index-s4]
  - why: No one loop is applied to every entrant; the scaffold differs by model and changed in 2026, and board rows name products and scaffolds (Manus 1.5, claude-opus-4-6 (CoWork)).
  > The leaderboard reports the single best performance for each agent, regardless of environment.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `human-expert` · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
  - why: The professionals' deliverables are the reference, fixed at 100% (and Elo 1,000); they are not scored as entrants.
  > We canonicalize scores so that the human baseline Elo is fixed at 1,000.

**Open review checks** (12):

1. (field `domain`) Family. RLI is the taxonomy's own example for society-econ-law, and OSWorld 2.0 its near miss in agents-tooluse. The entry reads RLI's scored quantity as the economic value of the output (a client's acceptance against a professional's paid deliverable), with long-horizon-autonomy secondary. 2. (field `data.size`) The denominator. The paper and the board say the 230 private projects carry every quantitative score, but every published rate read here is a whole multiple of 1/240, not 1/230 (21.25% is 51/240, 2.5% is 6/240, 0.83% is 2/240; our arithmetic, not a quoted figure). Whether the rates are computed over all 240 projects should be confirmed before any claim is stored. · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]

The July 2026 results run Anthropic and OpenAI models in Claude Code and Codex CLI with computer use, up to 24 hours, $50 per project ($150 for one model) and a worker-critic loop; the release rows used Scale AI's computer-use scaffold or OpenHands, one hour and $30. The board mixes both with no label. The entry records this as conditions with versions empty; a reviewer may prefer a revision with version\_kind. · [S3][remote-labor-index-s3]

   > All evaluations are therefore performed manually by trained experts using a specialized platform.
5. (field `evaluation_method`) pairwise-preference-elo is rejected because the published headline is the automation rate. If the paper's Elo results (seven agents, human baseline 1,000) are catalogued, the method should be added with comparability.rating\_pool\_required. · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
   > For each project, a deliverable from two different AIs is presented to human evaluators
6. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type nonprofit follows the term's holder rule (CAIS holds the public set and repository). No source says who holds the private 230 projects or the evaluator workforce's contracts; if Scale AI holds the private set, industry-lab is the better reading.
7. (field `governance.independence_flags`) Independence. No source read says whether Scale AI sells data or evaluation services to developers whose agents it ranks, or whether a ranked developer funds RLI. evaluator-sells-evaluations and funded-by-evaluated-party are unset pending a source; the board itself is Scale's. · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
   > For models that support computer-use, we used a computer-use scaffold developed by Scale AI.
8. (field `data.data_provenance`) The paper gives two counts of eligible Upwork categories, 43 after filtering and 45 in its appendix; 23 categories survive in the final set either way. · [S2][remote-labor-index-s2]
   > This left us with 45 total Upwork categories to source projects from.
9. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) ceiling\_anchor\_type expert-average reads the professionals' deliverables as the parity reference. Each was checked during cleaning to complete its project, which could instead be read as a measured-ceiling (100% shown reachable).
10. (field `aggregation_policy`) The board's Cost Savings is defined as an average across projects; the paper's autoflation is the reduction in the cost of the whole bundle. The two may not be the same quantity. Grok 4, in the paper's table and in CAIS's 2026 chart, is absent from the board read here. · [S4][remote-labor-index-s4]

12. (field `released`) Epoch's export lists the Remote Labor Index with its Score column (its source for current use), and the stub's date, 2025-10-29, is a day before the arXiv v1 used for released. · [S7][remote-labor-index-s7]

### 2.2 StockNet (stocknet)

`data/benchmarks/society-econ-law/stocknet.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-08 · last verified 2026-11-08

*Binary next-day movement of 88 US stocks from tweets and five days of prices, 2014-2015, scored by accuracy and MCC.*

A dataset for predicting whether a stock's adjusted closing price rises or falls on a target trading day, from the tweets that mention its ticker and its historical prices over the preceding five-day lag. It covers 88 US stocks, all eight in the Conglomerates sector and the ten largest by capital in each of the other eight, from 2014-01-01 to 2016-01-01; tweets were retrieved by ticker regex and prices taken from Yahoo Finance. Movements between -0.5% and 0.55% were removed to balance the classes, leaving 26,614 targets (49.78% fall, 50.22% rise), split by time into 20,339 for training, 2,555 for development and 3,720 for test (October to December 2015). Scores are accuracy and the Matthews correlation coefficient on the test set. The paper introduced its own generative model, StockNet, whose full variant scored 58.23% accuracy and 0.0808 MCC against 50.89% for a random guess and 57.64% for the best baseline; the paper calls 56% a satisfying result for the task. The data and model code sit on the first author's GitHub account under MIT licences, unchanged since 2018. There is no leaderboard; others report results in their own papers, and FinBen carries a prompt-formatted copy for evaluating language models.

**Open review checks** (12):

1. (field `id`) The id stocknet is proposed from the paper's and repository's name; allocation is a human act. ACL18 is the name FinBen and its Hugging Face copy use, and the model shares the name StockNet. A reviewer may prefer acl18 as the id.
2. (field `capability`) capability carries context-integration only, and only loosely, because no term names predicting a financial quantity from a time series; scientific-prediction is limited to physical, chemical, biological and Earth systems. The gap is logged in taxonomy/\_failures; widening scientific-prediction or adding a forecasting-of-series term is the call.
3. (field `domain.primary`) The domain search found no time-series family; the only forecasting leaves outside society-econ-law are earth-climate's weather and energy ones. A future general time-series family could claim this entry.
4. (field `designed_for_subjects`) designed\_for\_subjects adds classical-algorithm for the random-guess and ARIMA baselines. ARIMA is fitted to each series, which the term's inclusion test allows for fitted constants; drop it if baselines should not count. · [S1][stocknet-s1]
   > RAND: a naive predictor making random guess in up or down.
5. (field `data.data_provenance`) data\_provenance tags Yahoo Finance prices as curated-public-database. Its exclusion sends harvested web content to web-scraped; whether a commercial price-history service is a curated archive or web content is a judgement.
6. (field `data.upstream_licences`) The dataset redistributes tweets, raw as full tweet JSON and preprocessed with the user id, under an MIT licence; the paper says Twitter data were accessed under Twitter's licence. Whether the redistribution and the personal data it carries suit the catalogue's dataset\_url is for a reviewer. · S4
   > Keys: 'text', 'user\\\_id\\\_str', 'created\\\_at'
7. (field `lineage.forks`) FinBen's copy is recorded as a fork with id finben, not yet catalogued. Its splits keep the paper's development and test counts but its training split has 442 more rows, and its prompts were not read (the record is gated). Whether FinBen should be catalogued as a suite that contains this task, rather than as a fork, is the call. · [S2][stocknet-s2]
   > "name":"test","num\_bytes":13359338,"num\_examples":3720
8. (field `governance.independence_flags`) The Bloomberg grant is recorded as funding without a flag, because the paper evaluates no Bloomberg system. A reviewer may weigh that Bloomberg sells market data and analytics. · [S1][stocknet-s1]
   > This research was supported by a grant from Bloomberg
9. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk is medium. For prompted language models trained after 2015 the test outcomes are public market history; no source evidencing memorisation was read, which high would need.
10. (field `released`) released is 2018-07-15, the first day of the conference as the PDF's footer gives it; the Anthology dates the paper to July 2018 only, and the data were public on GitHub from 2018-04-28 (GitHub API, not a quoted Source). The data's first commit is the alternative. · [S8][stocknet-s8]
   > Month: July Year: 2018
11. (field `as_used`) Only the 2025 paper's abstract page was read; that it uses the paper's test split, and its numbers, are not checked. The as\_used row says so.
12. (field `comparability.material_extra`) The five-day lag window, fixed by the paper's sample construction, and the class thresholds have no condition field; a variant that changes either is a different task. No EvalConditions record was written. · [S1][stocknet-s1]
   > We use a 5-day lag window for sample construction

### 2.3 Finance Agent Benchmark (finance-agent-benchmark)

`data/benchmarks/society-econ-law/finance-agent-benchmark.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-08 · last verified 2026-11-08

*Analyst questions over SEC filings, answered by a model with tools and judged against expert rubrics; private test set.*

A benchmark from Vals AI of the research an entry-level financial analyst does on public companies' SEC filings. Experts from banks, hedge funds and private equity wrote each question with a reference answer, the documents needed and the steps to the answer, and a second expert reviewed it. A model answers inside Vals' own agent harness, which gives it tools to search EDGAR and the web, fetch and parse pages and query what it stored (v2 adds a calculator and price history), and its final answer is graded by an LLM judge against rubric checks drawn from the expert's answer, with a check that nothing contradicts it. v1 (May 2025) has 537 questions in nine categories, from quantitative retrieval to market analysis; 50 are public under CC BY 4.0, 150 form a private validation set Vals licenses, and 337 are a test set that never leaves Vals. v1.1 (early 2026) re-dated questions, moved search to Tavily and judged by the mode of three GPT-5.2 calls. v2 replaced the questions and taxonomy (27 public, 450 private validation, 450 test), added dealbreaker-gated partial credit and a three-model jury, and runs each model three times; v2.1 (November 2026) fixed questions and rubrics, changed the jury and fails hedged answers, on 449 test questions. Every published score is on the private test set, run by Vals on its leaderboard. The paper's best model, o3, scored 46.8%; on v2.1 the top score is 67.85%.

#### finance-agent-benchmark · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary society-econ-law/financial-analysis; secondary agents-tooluse/tool-api-calling, language/retrieval-qa · [S3][finance-agent-benchmark-s3]
  - why: The scored quantity is the correctness of a financial analyst's answer about public companies, checked criterion by criterion against an expert's answer, which is the financial-analysis leaf's definition (analytical questions over financial documents and statements). The family's exclusion for autonomous operation does not fit, because nothing about the operation is scored. The harness is Vals' own and fixed for every model, tool calls and turns are reported but not graded, and no environment state is checked; the paper's conclusion states its finding as a limit of financial analysis capability. The model reaches the filings only through API tools (tool-api-calling, as secondary), and it must find the evidence among public filings before answering (retrieval-qa, as for FinanceBench).
  > Finance Agent Benchmark demonstrates significant limitations in current AI financial analysis capabilities.
- `capability` = tool-use · [S3][finance-agent-benchmark-s3]
  - why: The questions concern filings published from 2024 on, which the model can reach only through the harness's EDGAR, search, parse and retrieve tools; the paper attributes the worst results to misused tools (hallucinated documents, repeated failing calls).
  > This harness allows the models to be evaluated in an environment where they had access to a set of tools that is sufficient to produce an accurate response.
- `capability` = quantitative-reasoning · [S3][finance-agent-benchmark-s3]
  - why: Most categories end in a computed figure (a CAGR, an adjusted EBITDA, a beat or miss against guidance, M&A capacity), and the expert's solution steps include the calculation; v1.1's prompt asks for two decimal places without rounding intermediate values.
  > Each question underwent peer review by a different expert to verify calculations and content validity.
- `capability` = factual-precision · [S3][finance-agent-benchmark-s3]
  - why: The judge checks each key point of the expert's answer separately (figures, dates and named facts), plus a check that nothing in the answer contradicts it, rather than one verdict on the whole.
  > Rather than evaluating answers holistically, we separate assessment into distinct rubrics that align with specific key points from expert answers
- `evaluation_method` = rubric-graded, model-graded-judge · [S4][finance-agent-benchmark-s4]
  - why: Named criteria from the expert's answer are checked one by one and combined (all must pass in v1; a dealbreaker-gated, severity-weighted share in v2), and an LLM judge or jury applies them, so both terms apply.
  > Each question is composed of weighted checks, and a subset are flagged as dealbreakers
- `designed_for_subjects` = model-in-benchmark-harness · [S5][finance-agent-benchmark-s5]
  - why: Vals runs every model in its own ReAct-style harness with one prompt and toolset, and each leaderboard row names a model; the methodology page states the purpose of the fixed harness.
  > Models are called through a fixed harness that we control, so that differences in scores reflect the model rather than the scaffold.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `agents-tooluse/long-horizon-autonomy` · [S4][finance-agent-benchmark-s4]
  - why: The agents-tooluse family was considered first as primary, against APEX-Agents, whose tool-using professional tasks went there (tool-api-calling, kept here as secondary). Its inclusion test's "result it returned" covers a final answer, but this grader scores the answer's financial content against an expert rubric, not whether functions were selected and invoked correctly, and Vals fixes the loop so that only the model varies; the v2.1 page states the purpose as automating analysts' work (review\_checks). Long-horizon autonomy in particular is not scored either, since each item is judged on its final answer.
  > Finance Agent v2.1 measures how well AI can aid analysts in automating busy work
- `domain` not `agents-tooluse/research-agents` · [S3][finance-agent-benchmark-s3]
  - why: The agent gathers from EDGAR and the web, but every v2 question has one determinate answer, not an open research question, and the sources the agent cites are not scored.
  > although we asked models to provide citations or sources for their answers, we did not evaluate the accuracy or reliability of these sources.
- `domain` not `society-econ-law/economically-valuable-work` · [S3][finance-agent-benchmark-s3]
  - why: The questions are analysts' work, and the paper compares the agents' time and cost with the experts', but the leaf is defined by expert comparison against human work product, and here an LLM judge checks rubric criteria; financial-analysis is the narrower fit.
  > compared to human experts requiring 16.8 minutes and costing $25.66
- `capability` not `knowledge-recall` · [S3][finance-agent-benchmark-s3]
  - why: The experts wrote questions on documents published no earlier than 2024 so that the answer comes from the filings, not from training data.
  > The experts focused their question generation on documents published no earlier than 2024 (after most training cutoffs).
- `designed_for_subjects` not `agent-scaffold` · [S4][finance-agent-benchmark-s4]
  - why: The v2 README says how to swap in one's own harness, and the v2.1 page says the time limit lets different agent implementations be compared, but no row on the boards read varies the loop.
  > A fixed time budget also allows us to normalize and compare performance across different agent implementations.

### 2.4 StockBench (stockbench)

`data/benchmarks/society-econ-law/stockbench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-08 · last verified 2026-11-08

*LLM agents trade 20 Dow Jones stocks daily over four months of 2025 data, scored on return, drawdown and Sortino ratio.*

A benchmark from Tsinghua University and Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications in which a language model acts as a stock-trading agent in a back-trading environment built from real market data. The agent starts with $100,000 in cash and, at each market open over 82 trading days (3 March to 30 June 2025), sees prices, its holdings and recent actions, and up to five news articles from the previous 48 hours for each of the 20 highest-weighted stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average; it picks stocks for a closer look at their fundamentals, then sets a dollar target for each stock (increase, decrease or hold), which the environment converts into shares at the opening price. Every model runs inside the benchmark's own fixed four-step workflow. A run is scored on final return, maximum drawdown and Sortino ratio, averaged over three runs, and models are ranked by the mean of the three metrics' z-scores, so a rank depends on the other models in the table. An equal-weight buy-and-hold portfolio is the reference (0.4% return, -15.2% drawdown); in the paper most of 13 models beat it on return, by at most about two percentage points. The environment replays history, so the agent's trades never move prices. Code and the cached market data are public under Apache-2.0, for non-commercial research.

- `self_description` · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  > we introduce STOCKBENCH, a contamination-free benchmark designed to evaluate LLM agents in realistic, multi-month stock trading environments
- `released` = 2025-10-02 · [S2][stockbench-s2]
  > Submitted on 2 Oct 2025 (v1), last revised 2 Mar 2026 (this version, v2)

#### stockbench · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary society-econ-law/trading-market-interaction · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  - why: The agent acts inside a market environment -- buying, selling and holding stocks against real prices -- and the scored quantities are the outcome of that trading, the portfolio's return, drawdown and risk-adjusted return, which is the trading-market-interaction leaf and the family's inclusion test (the scored quantity concerns markets). The paper's claim is profitability and risk management, not the operation of an interface.
  > Performance is measured using financial metrics such as cumulative return, maximum drawdown, and the Sortino ratio, capturing both profitability and risk management.
- `capability` = optimization · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  - why: The benchmark states its objectives (profit and risk control, measured by return, drawdown and Sortino ratio) and ranks systems by how well they achieve them, through the z-score aggregate; no answer key exists.
  > Models are ranked based on the z-score aggregation of all three metrics.
- `capability` = context-integration · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  - why: The environment supplies the prices, news and fundamentals each decision is made from, and the paper's ablation shows that removing the news and then the fundamentals lowers the return, so the score depends on using the supplied material.
  > cumulative returns drop as news and then fundamentals are removed, confirming their importance
- `evaluation_method` = domain-metric, entrant-relative-ranking · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  - why: Maximum drawdown and the Sortino ratio are measures standardised in finance, which the paper cites to that literature, and the published rank z-scores each metric against the field of entrants, so adding a model moves every other model's rank with no change to its runs, the inclusion case of entrant-relative-ranking.
  > Models are ranked based on the z-score aggregation of all three metrics.
- `designed_for_subjects` = model-in-benchmark-harness, classical-algorithm · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  - why: The workflow is held fixed and minimal so that only the backbone model varies, and the buy-and-hold strategy is implemented as the reference row.
  > As a reference point, we implement a passive equal-weight buy-and-hold strategy

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `agents-tooluse/long-horizon-autonomy` · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  - why: The family's near miss (osworld-2-0) and vending-bench-2 score what an autonomous loop achieved with tools; here the agent chooses no tools and runs no loop of its own. Each day the benchmark's fixed workflow hands it the data and takes back a decision per stock, and the score is the portfolio's market outcome, so the subject is the economic result rather than autonomous operation, and the society-econ-law exclusion does not apply.
  > We keep the workflow minimal, since overly complicated workflows introduce inductive biases that may favor certain backbone LLMs.
- `domain` not `games-planning/open-ended-environments` · [S3][stockbench-s3]
  - why: Each run is a long episode, but games-planning's test needs an environment that responds, and this one replays recorded prices that the agent's trades do not affect; the goal (profit with controlled risk) is also fixed, not open-ended.
  > Even there, the environment does not push back, as StockBench replays real markets the agent
- `domain` not `society-econ-law/finance-forecasting` · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  - why: The agent never states a predicted price, return or volatility; it sets positions, and only the realised portfolio outcome is scored.
  > choosing between three actions: (1) increase, (2) decrease, or (3) hold the position
- `domain` not `society-econ-law/financial-analysis` · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  - why: The paper's contrast is with static financial question answering; no question is posed or answered.
  > showing that strong performance on static financial question-answering do not necessarily translate into effective trading behavior
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  - why: The paper compares rankings over a downturn and an upturn window as an analysis, but the benchmark's scores come from one window, not from a deliberately shifted one.
  > all LLM agents underperform the passive baseline during the downturn but outperform it in the upturn
- `capability` not `quantitative-reasoning` · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  - why: The paper counts arithmetic errors in share quantities, but the scored output is a portfolio outcome, not a number the agent computes, and the environment converts dollar targets into shares itself.
  > the decisions are executed by converting dollar targets into share quantities based on the opening price
- `designed_for_subjects` not `agent-scaffold` · S4
  - why: The README invites custom trading agents, but the paper and the leaderboard evaluate backbones in the fixed workflow only, and no ranked row is an outside agent.
  > Extend the platform with your own trading strategies by implementing custom agents.

#### stockbench · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system Kimi-K2 · [S6][stockbench-s6]
  > 1 Kimi-K2 +1.9 -11.8 0.0420
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = true · S5
  - why: The code and the cached market data are public, the backbones are API or open-weight models, and an independent port reproduces the paper's baseline row exactly from them.
  > The buy-and-hold baseline comes out at 0.4% return, -15.2% max drawdown and Sortino 0.0155. That matches Table 2 of the paper.
- `task` = exists true; input each trading day at market open, for each of the 20 stocks, the opening price, the agent's current holdings, its actions on held stocks over the previous seven days, and up to five news articles from the previous 48 hours, for the stocks the agent selects, fundamentals (market capitalisation, P/E ratio, dividend yield, 52-week high and low, recent quarterly dividends); output A decision for every stock -- increase, decrease or hold -- with a dollar target, revised when it exceeds the cash available, which the environment converts into shares at the opening price; then the simulation advances one day.; scoring Over the 82-day window, final return, maximum drawdown and Sortino ratio of the portfolio, each averaged over three runs with different seeds; models are ranked by the mean of the three z-scores across the table. · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  > If the decisions of the agents exceed available liquidity, the system flags the issue and requires the agent to revise its decisions until they can be executed within available resources.
- `execution.reproducibility_tier` = fully-automatable · S5
  - why: The code, the prompts and the cached data are public, and the backbones are API or open-weight models; an independent rerun reproduces the baseline row exactly.
  > The buy-and-hold baseline comes out at 0.4% return, -15.2% max drawdown and Sortino 0.0155. That matches Table 2 of the paper.
- `execution.harness` = \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\] · S4
  > bash scripts/run\_benchmark.sh
- `aggregation_policy` = official-aggregate · [S1][stockbench-s1]
  - why: The paper and the project page publish one rank per model, from the mean of the three metrics' z-scores, beside the three metrics themselves.
  > Models are ranked based on the z-score aggregation of all three metrics.

**Open review checks** (12):

1. (field `domain`) Placement. trading-market-interaction is primary because the scored quantities are market outcomes; agents-tooluse was rejected because the agent runs inside the benchmark's fixed workflow with no tools of its own, and games-planning because the replayed market does not respond. Confirm, and confirm that no secondary leaf is needed. · [S3][stockbench-s3]
   > Even there, the environment does not push back, as StockBench replays real markets the agent
2. (field `data.size`) The window is stated three ways. The paper's method gives 3 March to 30 June 2025 (82 trading days), its introduction "March 2025 to July 2025", the project page "March 1-June 30", and Figure 4's caption labels the downturn and upturn windows 2024 while its text says 2025. The Inspect port finds 83 days with price data and 86 simulated by the original code (holidays counted). · [S1][stockbench-s1]
   > The benchmark is instantiated using recent market data from March 2025 to July 2025 and will be continuously updated to prevent overlap with the training corpora of LLMs.
3. (field `evaluation_method`) The Sortino ratio's formula in the paper's text differs from the released code; the port says the baseline's 0.0155 reproduces only with the code's version. Which one defines the benchmark's metric matters for the Metric records still to be written. · S5
   > The released code, and this port, divide the mean daily return by the sample standard deviation of the negative daily returns.
4. (field `aggregation_policy`) The paper's composite is written z(Ret) - z(DD) + z(SR) while drawdowns are tabled as negative percentages; whether the sign penalises or rewards a shallower drawdown should be checked against the code. The project page calls the rank "the mean of all three metrics". · [S1][stockbench-s1]
   > z(Ret) − z(DD) + z(SR)
5. (field `governance.known_limitation`) The paper says trading costs are not modelled; the port says the released code charges a 1-basis-point commission on every order. known\_limitation quotes the paper. · S5
   > This port charges a 1 basis point commission on every order, as the released code does.
6. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium. The look-ahead the port reports (later 52-week highs and lows in the 3 March fundamentals snapshot; decision-day news in the original code) is future information given to every entrant, not a training route; a reviewer may want it as a known\_limitation or as evidence for high. · S5
   > The fundamentals snapshots are not point-in-time.
7. (field `data.refresh`) refresh static, against the paper's promise of a continuously updated window. If the authors release a new window, the family needs versions (an edition per window) and refresh versioned-releases or periodic-recompetition. · [S1][stockbench-s1]
   > It is worth noting that we will continuously update the back-trading environment to avoid overlap with the training corpora of contemporary LLMs.
8. (field `evaluation_method`) evaluation\_method is domain-metric and entrant-relative-ranking. episodic-return could be added for final return (cumulative, unbounded); domain-metric's "named and standardised within a discipline" is read to cover maximum drawdown and the Sortino ratio. No Metric records exist for the three measures, so headline\_metric and metrics are unset.
9. (field `comparability`) (domain-metric, classical-algorithm) resolves eligibility-gated, whose training-data fields have no counterpart in StockBench, as glee's entry also records; classical-algorithm rests on the buy-and-hold row being ranked in the table.
10. (field `data.data_provenance`) data\_provenance curated-public-database (vendor prices and fundamentals) and web-scraped (news via a search API); neither definition was written for commercial market-data feeds.
11. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type academic-lab or individual (code in the first author's personal account, written during an internship). Independence was not assessed; whether any ranked model's developer has ties to the maintainers should be checked against a source before a flag is set.
12. (field `lineage`) The Inspect port is recorded in as\_used. It is a separately maintained derivative by another party that changes the calendar and the news window, so 04 S4 might make it a fork with its own id; its repository is one person's account, so the maintainer would need a neutral description. · S5
   > The original treats Good Friday, Memorial Day and Juneteenth as trading days, so it simulates 86 days.

### 2.5 BigLaw Bench (biglaw-bench)

`data/benchmarks/society-econ-law/biglaw-bench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-08 · last verified 2026-11-08

*Harvey's private law-firm tasks, from memos to deal analysis, scored by lawyer-written rubrics.*

Harvey's benchmark of legal work of the kind billed at large law firms. Harvey's legal research team, attorneys from BigLaw firms, turned time entries into tasks, each a prompt with the public documents it needs (some need none), split into litigation and transactional work and by task type: drafting, corporate advising, filings analysis, case management, research, due diligence and others. Each task has its own rubric. Required points earn positive scores weighted by importance; hallucinations, extraneous material and similar failures lose points. The answer score is the net points over the points available, read as the share of a lawyer-quality work product the system completes, and a source score counts how many correct statements cite their document. The core set is 100 tasks. Harvey keeps it private and runs every evaluation, scoring foundation models beside its own systems; the full data is available only by contacting Harvey. Six sample tasks with rubrics are on GitHub, and a 2026 academic study released 30 tasks with Harvey's permission. Later tracks added SPA deal-point extraction (Workflows), legal retrieval (Retrieval), lawyers' pairwise preferences rated by Elo (Arena), tasks for the UK, Australia and Spain (Global) and agentic US case-law research (Research). Harvey still reports core scores for new models in 2026, near 90% and above.

**Evidence** (50 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### biglaw-bench · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][biglaw-bench-s1]
  > a public-facing version of our internal dataset for evaluating large language models (LLMs) and model systems on complex legal tasks
- `released` = 2024-08-29 · [S1][biglaw-bench-s1]
  > Aug 29, 2024

#### biglaw-bench · Domain and capabilities

- `domain.primary` = society-econ-law/legal-document · [S1][biglaw-bench-s1]
  - why: The core tasks are prompt and document pairs whose output is a legal work product (a memo, a client alert, board resolutions, an analysis of filings or transcripts), and the rubric scores that product's substance, structure and style. The Workflows and Retrieval tracks extract from and search legal documents. That is drafting, reviewing and extracting from legal documents, the leaf's definition.
  > By converting time entries into model-based tasks (prompt / document pairs), we are able to identify and evaluate how models can contribute to real, high-value legal work.
- `domain.secondary` = society-econ-law/legal-reasoning, society-econ-law/economically-valuable-work · [S1][biglaw-bench-s1]
  - why: legal-reasoning because many rubric points check that the output applies a rule to the facts correctly, and Harvey reads score gains as better recall and application of legal principles; the Research track is legal research. economically-valuable-work because the tasks are converted from the time entries of billed legal work and the score is the share of a lawyer-quality work product completed. It is secondary because the score is a rubric's, not a comparison with a professional's own work product (review\_checks).
  > In defining benchmark tasks, we draw on a familiar feature of the legal profession: the time entry.
- `capability` = context-integration · [S1][biglaw-bench-s1]
  - why: Most tasks supply the documents the answer rests on (trial exhibits, filings, precedent agreements), and rubric points check the particulars drawn from them, such as a termination fee.
  > constructed using publicly available documents to enable transparent evaluation under realistic conditions
- `capability` = factual-precision · [S1][biglaw-bench-s1]
  - why: Rubric points check asserted particulars one by one, every hallucination is a negative point, and the source score checks each substantive statement for an accurate citation.
  > Negative criteria, such as hallucinations, were assigned negative scores
- `capability` = knowledge-recall · [S2][biglaw-bench-s2]
  - why: Some tasks have no document, so their rubric points on the law (procedure, evidence, corporate rules) can only be met from what the model holds; Harvey reads the score gains as better recall of legal principles.
  > All triplets have a prompt and a rubric, but some do not have a document as the associated legal task may not require one.
- `evaluation_method` = rubric-graded, exact-match, model-graded-judge, classification-metric, pairwise-preference-elo, human-expert-eval · [S1][biglaw-bench-s1]
  - why: Each task's rubric names points individually, with weights and negative points, and they are combined into the answer score, which is rubric-graded's inclusion case.
  > Answer score is computed by taking the combination of these positive and negative points and dividing by the total number of positive points available for a task.
- `designed_for_subjects` = instruction-tuned-model, full-product-pipeline, tool-augmented-model · [S3][biglaw-bench-s3]
  - why: Harvey prompts public foundation models directly with the task and its documents (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, then GPT-5-series, Claude and Gemini models) and scores its own shipped Assistant systems beside them; the Research track gives models search tools.
  > Models must use tools to perform searches in order to identify relevant research context and provide a grounded, cited response.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `agents-tooluse/research-agents` · [S1][biglaw-bench-s1]
  - why: Only the Research track gives the model search tools, and Harvey says the core tasks need no multi-part or agentic workflow; the leaf is the Research subset's secondary instead.
  > tasks that we use to test fundamental model capabilities to solve problems involving reasoning about, analyzing, and discussing legal concepts and text without the need for multi-part or agentic workflows
- `capability` not `instruction-following` · [S1][biglaw-bench-s1]
  - why: Rubrics give structure and style points (a memo format, a professional tone) and penalise wrong tone or length, but these serve the work product; the score is not compliance with stated constraints.
  > They also penalize common LLM failure modes such as incorrect tone or length, irrelevant material, toxicity, and hallucinations.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `human-expert` · [S4][biglaw-bench-s4]
  - why: Arena pits systems against humans, but no human score is published, and the core benchmark has no human entrant.
  > competing against foundation models, internal prototypes, and even humans

#### biglaw-bench · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system Fable 5 · [S6][biglaw-bench-s6]
  > In our internal evaluation using BigLaw Bench, Harvey's proprietary legal benchmark, Fable 5 scored 93.4% overall
- `ground_truth_source` = expert-panel · [S2][biglaw-bench-s2]
  - why: The rubrics were written by Harvey's attorneys and reviewed by other legal experts; the grader applies them, it does not define them.
  > Rubrics are task-specific and were developed by legal experts, then later reviewed by other legal experts.

### 2.6 GLEE (glee)

`data/benchmarks/society-econ-law/glee.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Two-player bargaining, negotiation and persuasion games in language, scored on self-gain, efficiency and fairness.*

GLEE (Games in Language-based Economic Environments) is a framework and benchmark in which two players, language models or people, play sequential economic games and may attach free-text messages to their moves. It has three families taken from economic theory: bargaining over the division of a sum that shrinks with every round of delay (after Rubinstein), negotiation between a seller and a buyer over the price of one good (bilateral trade), and repeated persuasion, in which a seller who knows each product's quality sends a message before the buyer decides (cheap talk). Each family is parameterised by horizon, information (whether a player knows the other's preferences), whether messages are allowed, stakes, and discount factors or valuations. A game is scored by each player's self-gain and by the outcome's efficiency and fairness, most of them normalised to \[0, 1\]. The paper ran 13 LLMs in all 169 pairings across 1,320 configurations (about 80K games) inside its own fixed-prompt game manager, and 3,405 crowdworkers played against Gemini-1.5-flash. Results are linear-regression estimates per family, role and metric that control for configuration and opponent, so a model's number depends on whom it played. The GLEE Competition (August 2026, the IAB workshop at NeurIPS 2026) put agents and humans in one live matchmaking pool, rated by opponent-adjusted payoff percentiles.

**Evidence** (42 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### glee · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][glee-s1]
  > we introduce a benchmark for standardizing research on two-player, sequential, language-based games
- `released` = 2024-10-07 · [S2][glee-s2]
  > Submitted on 7 Oct 2024

#### glee · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary society-econ-law/economics-simulation; secondary games-planning/multi-agent-social · [S1][glee-s1]
  - why: Two family tests pass. The scores come from games against an opponent that responds (games-planning), and what they measure is the economic outcome of market-like exchanges, self-gain, efficiency and fairness (society-econ-law). The benchmark's own claim decides; it models LLMs as economic agents in parameterised economic environments and measures how market parameters shape the outcome, the economics-simulation leaf. The persuasion family's repeated cheap talk turns on reputation and trust, the social dynamics of the secondary leaf.
  > our focus extends to evaluating the outcome reached by the strategic behavior of the agents, using the fundamental economic notions of efficiency and fairness
- `capability` = planning · [S1][glee-s1]
  - why: Each game is an interactive episode against an explicit objective, the player's payoff, and the payoff scores the sequence of offers, decisions and messages the player made. The paper ties the horizon parameter to planning.
  > This factor influences the strategies agents adopt, particularly in terms of long-term planning and anticipation of future moves
- `capability` = communication · [S1][glee-s1]
  - why: In persuasion the seller's payoff is whether the buyer buys after reading its message, so the score depends on what the recipient did, not on the message itself. The term holds for that family only.
  > Alice gets a utility of 1 if Bob buys (regardless of the true product quality), and 0 otherwise
- `capability` = collaboration · [S1][glee-s1]
  - why: Bargaining and negotiation are mixed-motive, since delay shrinks the bargaining pot and a price between the two valuations gains both sides, and efficiency and fairness score the outcome the two players reach together. The paper claims that language serves coordination toward mutually beneficial outcomes.
  > so language becomes essential for coordination, signaling intentions, and achieving mutually beneficial outcomes
- `evaluation_method` = simulation-rollout, tournament-play · [S1][glee-s1]
  - why: Each game is run in GLEE's game engine and scored per game on bounded measures (all but negotiation's fairness normalised to \[0, 1\]). The LLMs play every pairing, and the published estimates are fitted to those games, so a model's number depends on the pool; the paper finds no model best against all opponents. The 2026 competition rated agents and humans from games in one shared pool.
  > The 169 possible pairs (including a language model playing against itself, with attention to the assignment for Alice or Bob) played across 1,320 different configurations
- `designed_for_subjects` = model-in-benchmark-harness, multi-agent-system, classical-algorithm, human-nonexpert · S4
  - why: The competition's agent track admits any decision procedure, from prompted LLMs to classical game-theoretic solvers, each an independent agent negotiating with others, and its human track scores people on the same scale.
  > Nothing constrains how it decides: a prompted LLM, a fine-tuned one, a classical game-theoretic solver, or any mix of them.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `games-planning/game-theory` · [S1][glee-s1]
  - why: The paper reviews each family's equilibria, but no score is computed against a solution concept; players are scored on their payoffs against the other players in the pool, which the leaf's definition puts outside it.
  > the cheap-talk game only admits a babbling equilibrium
- `evaluation_method` not `domain-metric` · [S1][glee-s1]
  - why: Efficiency and fairness are economic notions, but GLEE defines its own formulas for them (bargaining fairness is one minus four times the squared distance of the share from one half), not measures standardised within economics, which the term asks for.
  > Metrics are normalized to \[0, 1\], such that higher values indicate better (more efficient or fair) outcomes
- `evaluation_method` not `human-distribution-percentile` · [S3][glee-s3]
  - why: The competition turned each payoff into a percentile, but against every payoff on that configuration and role, earned by LLMs, agents and humans alike, not against a measured human population.
  > After each game your payoff is converted to a percentile against every payoff earned on the SAME configuration in the SAME role (seeded by the GLEE research dataset, joined by competition games as they are played).
- `designed_for_subjects` not `instruction-tuned-model` · [S1][glee-s1]
  - why: Its exclusion applies; GLEE's game manager drives each model across turns.
  > Each time the language model is required to make a decision (of any type), the language model receives a message containing all the information that has accumulated since its previous turn

#### glee · Data and licence

- `as_used` = protocol ARIA (Fudan University and ByteDance Seed) trains language agents with reinforcement learning and evaluates them on 48 GLEE bargaining and negotiation configurations, each role played 25 times against fixed opponents, reporting a win rate (a higher payoff than the opponent in bargaining, a better price in negotiation) rather than GLEE's self-gain, efficiency or fairness. · [S5][glee-s5]
  > following GLEE \[43\], we evaluate ARIA across 48 game configurations
- `data.access` = generated-on-demand · [S1][glee-s1]
  - why: The scored items are games that two players produce afresh in the GLEE engine, on configurations drawn from a parameter grid, so no fixed item set exists. The paper's game records are public (records\_access).
  > is infinite for each of the game families, it is clear that data cannot be collected from all possible games
- `data.records_access` = fully-open · [S1][glee-s1]

- `data.refresh` = versioned-releases · [S3][glee-s3]
  - why: The paper's protocol is fixed in its arXiv versions (v3 is the one read), and the 2026 competition was a dated edition with its own grid and scoring. Within the competition's 29 days the pool, and so every rating, moved continuously.

  - why: The paper publishes the crowdworkers' self-gain beside the LLMs' (the human row of Table 6) and asks how LLMs compare with them. ### 2.7 MathTutorBench (mathtutorbench)

`data/benchmarks/society-econ-law/mathtutorbench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*LLM math tutors scored on expertise, student understanding and pedagogy; a trained reward model judges scaffolding.*

An open-source benchmark from ETH Zurich for dialog tutoring models, built from existing math tutoring data: GSM8K word problems, StepVerify's teacher-annotated student solutions, and the teacher turns of MathDial and Bridge, combined as MathDialBridge. Seven tasks sit under three teacher skills. Math expertise is problem solving (final-answer accuracy) and Socratic questioning (BLEU of generated sub-questions against GSM8K's). Student understanding is judging whether a student's solution is correct (F1), locating its first wrong step (micro-F1), and solving correctly despite a student's wrong answer in the dialog (accuracy). Pedagogy is writing the next teacher turn of a dialog, with a simple prompt (scaffolding generation) or with LearnLM's pedagogical prompt (pedagogical instruction following), each on a base split and on a hard split with longer dialogs. The four pedagogy scores are win rates, the share of a model's turns that a released reward model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct fine-tuned on pedagogical preference pairs) scores above the human teacher's turn; the paper validates it at 0.84 accuracy in preferring expert over novice teacher responses. The leaderboard in the README and on the site reports the nine columns with no aggregate, and has grown from the paper's eight models to seventeen.

  - why: What the benchmark is built to score is a tutor's teaching, the leaf's "teaching or assessing a learner, scored on pedagogical outcome or instructional quality", and its headline finding is that solving ability does not make a good tutor. The mathematics family's exclusion turns away maths that serves a question about another field. Two tasks (problem solving, mistake correction) do check a numeric answer to a grade-school word problem, which the secondary leaf records.
  > subject expertise, indicated by solving ability, does not immediately translate to good teaching
- `capability` = context-integration · [S3][mathtutorbench-s3]
  - why: The student-understanding and pedagogy tasks supply the student's solution or the dialog so far, and the answer depends on it; mistake location's answer is a step of the supplied solution.
  > ability to accurately identify the exact location of the first mistake in a student
- `capability` = quantitative-reasoning · [S3][mathtutorbench-s3]
  - why: Problem solving and mistake correction score the final numeric answer to multi-step word problems, reached by arithmetic.
  > We include a math word problem solving task that measures the accuracy of the final numeric answer
- `evaluation_method` = exact-match, reference-metric, classification-metric, model-derived-metric · [S4][mathtutorbench-s4]
  - why: Each column has its own metric. Problem solving and mistake correction compare the extracted number with the reference (as floats, within 1e-6). Socratic questioning is sentence BLEU against GSM8K's sub-questions. Solution correctness is binary F1 and mistake location micro-F1 against StepVerify's labels. The four pedagogy columns are win rates decided by a released reward model, which outputs a scalar for each response; it is not a general model prompted for a verdict.
  > Problem Solving: accuracy · Socratic Questioning: BLEU · Solution Correctness: F1 · Mistake Location: micro-F1 · Mistake Correction: accuracy · remaining columns: reward-model win rate.

1. (field `domain`) The primary family rests on the education-tutoring leaf's definition. 3. (field `evaluation_method`) model-derived-metric rather than model-graded-judge. The reward model takes a grading instruction as its system prompt but returns a scalar, and the win is a comparison of two scalars. · [S5][mathtutorbench-s5]
   > Judge the pedagogical quality of the responses provided by two teachers.
4. (field `data.dataset_licence`) The licence is recorded as CC-BY-4.0 from the paper and the README badge, but the README's closing line and the site's footer say CC BY-SA 4.0, and GitHub detects no licence file. · [S6][mathtutorbench-s6]
   > Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License
5. (field `governance.submission_process`) submission\_process is maintainer-verified, because the README says the maintainers will run a submitted model but not that they publish their own number; sandboxed-rerun if they do.
6. (field `governance.independence_flags`) grader-from-evaluated-party rests on the reward model and TutorRL-7B both sitting under eth-nlped, with the site marking "our models"; the Qwen base of the reward model is a weaker, second ground. · [S4][mathtutorbench-s4]
   > Red-edged stars mark our models.
7. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) ceiling\_anchor\_type expert-average treats MathDialBridge's teacher turns as an expert reference; Bridge's originals are novice teachers' turns that experts revised, and the sources do not say which version is the reference.
8. (field `data.refresh`) refresh static rests on datasets/ being unchanged since 2025-02-25. Commits on 2025-04-17 ("Fixed minor bugs") and 2025-09-05 touched configs and tasks, and one on 2026-07-30 touched the scoring script; none was audited for changes to scores.
9. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium. The paper calls GSM8K's test set contaminated without naming a route; high would need contamination\_evidence for the problem-solving split.

### 2.8 ObliQA (obliqa)

`data/benchmarks/society-econ-law/obliqa.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-08 · last verified 2026-11-08

*Compliance questions over Abu Dhabi financial regulation, scored on passage retrieval and on obligation coverage.*

ObliQA is a question-answering dataset for regulatory compliance, and RIRAG the task defined on it. Its 27,869 questions were generated by GPT-4 Turbo from obligation-bearing passages of the 40 financial regulation documents of Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM), about 640k words, framed as the questions a compliance officer would ask the regulator, and filtered by an NLI model; each question is linked to one to six source passages. ADGM experts reviewed 991 questions and judged 86.91% of their passages relevant. The task has two subtasks: retrieving the relevant passages from the whole corpus, scored by Recall@10 (MAP@10 as a diagnostic), and writing an answer from the retrieved passages, scored by RePASs. RePASs is reference-free: NLI models score how far each answer sentence is entailed by, or contradicts, the retrieved passages, and a fine-tuned LegalBERT classifier finds the obligation sentences whose coverage is checked; the three parts combine to a number between 0 and 1. The data (train, development and test splits) is open on GitHub and Hugging Face. The RIRAG-2025 shared task at the RegNLP 2025 workshop (COLING 2025) scored 19 teams on 446 further questions released without their passages, and a paper from one team showed that copying the retrieved obligations games RePASs.

**Evidence** (40 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### obliqa · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  > ObliQA - Obligatory Question-Answer dataset: We develop a multi-document, multipassage QA dataset1 specifically to facilitate research in RegNLP.
- `released` = 2024-09-09 · [S2][obliqa-s2]
  > Submitted on 9 Sep 2024 (v1), last revised 2 Dec 2024 (this version, v2)
- `lineage.variants` = id obliqa-mp; relation multi-passage extension; n_items 2976 · [S9][obliqa-s9]
  > we introduce ObliQA-MP, a dataset for multi-passage regulatory QA, extending the earlier ObliQA benchmark

#### obliqa · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary society-econ-law/policy-analysis; secondary language/retrieval-qa · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  - why: Every item is a regulatory question, what a regulated firm must do under a regulator's rules, and the answer is scored on whether it states all the applicable obligations without contradicting them, a measure the paper builds for regulatory compliance in place of general text-similarity metrics. The policy-analysis leaf names regulatory questions. Retrieval from the full corpus is half of the task and is scored on its own, the retrieval-qa leaf's case; FinanceBench takes the same pair with financial-analysis.
  > Imagine you are preparing a list of questions that a compliance officer at a company would ask regulatory authorities like the ADGM to clarify their understanding of compliance requirements and to ensure adherence to regulatory standards.
- `capability` = context-integration · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  - why: The corpus that determines every answer is supplied, the retrieval subtask scores whether the right passages were found in it, and RePASs scores the answer against the passages the system retrieved.
  > In the passage retrieval subtask, the system retrieves all relevant obligations from regulatory documents in response to a given question.
- `capability` = generation-fidelity · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  - why: RePASs compares the generated answer with its source passages, whose content it must preserve, sentence by sentence for entailment and contradiction and obligation by obligation for coverage.
  > The answer must cover all the obligations present in the source passages
- `evaluation_method` = classification-metric, model-derived-metric · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  - why: Retrieval is scored by Recall@10, with MAP@10 for diagnosis, statistics of the ranking against each question's linked passages. Answer generation is scored by RePASs, which released scoring models produce, an NLI cross-encoder for entailment and contradiction and a LegalBERT classifier, fine-tuned on GPT-4-labelled sentences, for obligations. The two subtasks are reported apart.
  > we use recall@10 as the main evaluation metric
- `designed_for_subjects` = retrieval-augmented-system, classical-algorithm · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  - why: The task's systems are retrieval-augmented pipelines; the paper's baseline fuses BM25 or a neural retriever with document ranking and passes the filtered passages to GPT-4 Turbo, and RePASs is computed against the passages the system itself retrieved.
  > Based on these filtered passages, we use the gpt-4-turbo-1106 model to generate comprehensive answers.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `society-econ-law/legal-document` · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  - why: The paper calls regulatory documents semi-legal texts, and retrieving and restating obligations from them is extraction from a legal document. But the items are questions about what compliance requires, not a document to review or draft, and the scored quantity is the answer's obligation coverage (review\_checks).
  > Regulatory documents are formal semi-legal texts issued by governmental regulatory bodies
- `domain` not `language/understanding` · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  - why: The family's exclusion of a general competence applied to domain text was weighed. The answer is not read off a supplied passage, the system must find the passages itself, and RePASs scores obligation coverage, which the paper calls specific to regulatory compliance.
  > In contrast, RePASs is tailored specifically to regulatory compliance.
- `evaluation_method` not `reference-metric` · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  - why: The paper reports BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore and others on its gold-standard answers only to argue that they miss obligation coverage, and RePASs is reference-free.
  > We propose a reference-free evaluation metric, RePASs, to evaluate generated answers in regulatory compliance contexts.
- `evaluation_method` not `composite` · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  - why: RePASs adds three components (entailment minus contradiction plus coverage, rescaled), but all three come from released scoring models, one method, which the term's exclusion leaves out; retrieval and generation are never combined into one number.
  > The score penalizes contradictions and normalizes the result between 0 and 1.

#### obliqa · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system BM25 (rank fusion) + GPT-4 Turbo (gpt-4-turbo-1106), the paper's baseline · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  > Based on these filtered passages, we use the gpt-4-turbo-1106 model to generate comprehensive answers.
- `ground_truth_source` = held-out-labels · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  > 991 questions and their associated passages from the ObliQA dataset were evaluated by ADGM experts
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = true · [S6][obliqa-s6]
  - why: The splits with their passages, the structured corpus and the RePASs code are public, so anyone can retrieve, generate and score on the test split. The shared task's hidden-set passages are not shown released in the sources read.
  > Run the evaluation script by providing your input JSON file and a group method name.
- `task` = exists true; input a compliance question about ADGM's financial regulation, the corpus of 40 structured ADGM regulatory documents, to retrieve from; output A ranked list of passage IDs (subtask 1) and an answer written from the retrieved passages (subtask 2), returned with the passages it used.; scoring Subtask 1 by Recall@10 (MAP@10 diagnostic) against the question's linked passages. Subtask 2 by RePASs, (Es - Cs + OCs + 1) / 3, where Es and Cs average each answer sentence's highest entailment and contradiction probability against the retrieved passages' sentences, and OCs is the share of the obligation sentences in those passages that some answer sentence entails above 0.7. · [S1][obliqa-s1]
  > The score penalizes contradictions and normalizes the result between 0 and 1.
- `execution.reproducibility_tier` = fully-automatable · [S6][obliqa-s6]
  - why: Data, passages, corpus and the RePASs scorer are public, and scoring needs no human or maintainer-held step for the test split. The obligation classifier is retrained locally from the README, so a rerun's RePASs depends on that training (review\_checks).
  > Run the training script to fine-tune LegalBERT on the provided dataset.
- `execution.harness` = RegNLP/RePASs (scripts/train\_model.py, then scripts/evaluate\_model.py on a JSON of questions, retrieved passages and answers) for answer generation; retrieval's Recall@10 and MAP@10 are standard computations over TREC-format runs, with no maintainer script in the sources read · [S6][obliqa-s6]
  > Run the evaluation script by providing your input JSON file and a group method name.
- `aggregation_policy` = none-by-design · [S3][obliqa-s3]
  - why: The paper and the shared task report retrieval (Recall@10, MAP@10) and answer generation (RePASs and its three components) in separate tables, with no combined score.
  > The evaluation of team submissions was conducted separately for both subtasks.

**Open review checks** (11):

1. (field `domain.primary`) Leaf call. policy-analysis rests on the items being regulatory questions, which its definition names. legal-document (extraction from semi-legal texts) is the nearest rival, and language/retrieval-qa could be primary if the family exclusion (a general competence on domain material) is read to cover regulatory RAG. ObliQA analyses no policy option. · [S1][obliqa-s1]
   > Regulatory documents are formal semi-legal texts issued by governmental regulatory bodies
2. (field `domain.primary`) The README lists policy analysis and impact assessment among the dataset's intended uses, but no ObliQA task scores the impact of a regulation; the leaf call rests on the regulatory questions alone, not on this line. · [S10][obliqa-s10]
   > Policy Analysis and Impact Assessment: Analyzing the potential impact of new or modified regulations.
3. (field `data.size`) The development split is 2,888 in the paper's Table 6, the README and the card, but 2,788 rows on Hugging Face, and 22,295 + 2,888 + 2,786 exceeds the stated 27,869 by 100. Which count is right, and whether the GitHub file matches the Hugging Face copy, was not checked. · [S5][obliqa-s5]
   > \- \*\*Validation:\*\* 2,888
4. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) RePASs can be gamed. Concatenating the obligation sentences that its own classifier picks from the retrieved passages scored a perfect or near-perfect RePASs, above the experts' 0.8101. Whether the answer-generation subset should carry a validity warning, and whether expert-average is still the right anchor, is a reviewer's call. · [S4][obliqa-s4]
   > this system achieves a perfect score, much higher than the score of human experts
5. (field `execution.reproducibility_tier`) The RePASs README has users fine-tune the LegalBERT obligation classifier themselves, so two reruns can score the same answers differently. Whether a released checkpoint exists (the paper links an ObligationClassifier repository, not read) decides whether fully-automatable should carry a caveat. · [S6][obliqa-s6]
   > Run the training script to fine-tune LegalBERT on the provided dataset.
6. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type community-collective rests on the RegNLP organisation having no stated holder; academic-lab if MBZUAI holds it.
7. (field `ground_truth_source`) Label quality. The maintainers' own ObliQA-MP paper says ObliQA relied on limited validation, and its LLM check found 20.46% of merged candidate passages not connected to their question after NLI filtering. That figure is for the multi-passage candidates, not ObliQA's test split. · [S9][obliqa-s9]
   > relied on limited validation procedures
8. (field `governance.independence_flags`) GPT-4 Turbo wrote the questions and is the baseline generator. No independence flag fits construction bias; a reviewer may want it recorded elsewhere.
9. (field `activity`) activity closed rests on the single 2024-25 shared task. The 2026 Hugging Face re-release cites a 2026 suite paper (not read) that may bring a new round. · [S5][obliqa-s5]
   > ObliQA is the \*\*Stage 1 / Tier 1\*\* dataset in the \*\*Synthetic Compliance for Regulatory RAG\*\* benchmark suite.
10. (field `versions`) Identity. The RIRAG-2025 hidden set (446 questions) is recorded as an event, not an edition; ObliQA-MP as a variant without an entry of its own. Either could be modelled differently.
11. (field `id`) Proposed id obliqa from the dataset's name; RIRAG, the task's name, is an alias. Allocation is a human act.

### 2.9 SimulacraBench (simulacrabench)

`data/benchmarks/society-econ-law/simulacrabench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*A NeurIPS 2026 competition: predict held-out survey answers on unreleased UNHCR, UNICEF and World Bank microdata.*

A NeurIPS 2026 competition that tests how well submitted systems stand in for hard-to-reach populations in behavioural surveys. Three unpublished instruments supply the data: UNHCR's ERPIS household survey of Syrian refugees in four countries of asylum, UNICEF's Faith & Immunisation survey of adults in ten countries, and the World Bank's Skills Assessment of job seekers, mostly in South Africa; together about 40,000 respondents in 14 countries. Each instrument is a respondent-by-question grid. Some respondents are visible in full; for the held-out ones only a few always-visible items are shown, and the system returns a probability distribution over every remaining item's options, including the option that the question was never asked under the survey's skip logic. Entrants upload code, not predictions, and the organisers run it with no network on one H100 against data that never leaves them. Each blank cell is scored by the log score, normalised per instrument so that a uniform guess scores 0 and perfection 1, and the Grand Prize ranks the plain mean of the three instruments' skills. Development-phase scores come back Laplace-noised and rounded to 0.01; the final phase scores one submission per team exactly, on respondents the development phase never touched. The public starter kit holds the schemas (question wording and options only), a generator of invented practice data, the grader and two baselines, a crowd marginal and an LLM prior.

### 2.10 ForecastBench (forecastbench)

`data/benchmarks/society-econ-law/forecastbench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-09-27 · last verified 2026-09-27

*LLMs and humans forecast real future events; scores update as the questions resolve.*

A benchmark run by the Forecasting Research Institute in which language models, and groups of superforecasters and members of the public, give probabilities for questions about future events. Questions come from two kinds of source: dataset questions generated from public time series with fixed templates, each asked at eight horizons from 7 days to 10 years, and market questions drawn from prediction platforms. New rounds of questions are released regularly and the leaderboards are recomputed nightly as questions resolve, so a score is provisional until every question behind it has resolved. Scores are Brier scores, adjusted for question difficulty and shown since 2026 as a Brier Index (0-100%, higher is better). There are separate leaderboards for out-of-the-box models (baseline), for open submissions that may use tools and scaffolds (tournament), and for early dataset-only results (preliminary). Known weaknesses the sources name: human groups were last surveyed in July 2024, so later models are compared with them through a fixed-effects adjustment rather than on the same questions.

**Reviewer checklist** for `forecastbench`:

- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist
